summary: This informational memo gathers the terms used to talk about provider-provisioned virtual private networks, where a service provider runs the VPN for customers. Several IETF working groups had proposed overlapping solutions, so the document sets a common vocabulary to avoid confusion.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC defines terms for VPN services that a network provider manages for customers. Its vocabulary distinguishes the kinds of service and the roles of customer and provider devices.

questions: what is a l2vpn or l3vpn
what is a provider provisioned vpn
what is the difference between vpls and vpws
subtitle: A vocabulary for provider-run virtual private network services and their components.

tldr.problem: Related provider-run VPN proposals used overlapping or inconsistent terms for services, devices, and network functions.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a vocabulary and groups VPN services into Layer 2 and Layer 3 types, then names their devices and building blocks.
tldr.outcome: It gives L2VPN and L3VPN work a shared terminology base and defines no protocol.

today: RFC 4026 is an Informational RFC published in March 2005. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why the Terms Need Clarifying
sections.content:
Many documents proposed services for provider-provisioned virtual private networks. Their ideas overlapped, and the same concept could have several names or one name could refer to different concepts.

This RFC gathers terms from relevant Internet-Drafts and RFCs to provide a common foundation for the L2VPN and L3VPN work. It arranges the terms as services, building blocks, functions, devices, and packet-switched network concepts.
sections.plainLanguage: Different documents sometimes used different words for the same network service. This RFC collects terms so readers can tell which service or device each word means.

sections.title: Layer 2 and Layer 3 VPN Services
sections.content:
A Layer 3 VPN connects hosts and routers using Layer 3 addresses. The RFC describes three Layer 2 VPN services: VPWS, VPLS, and IPLS. VPWS provides a point-to-point circuit between customer-edge devices. VPLS connects LAN segments so they behave as one LAN, with forwarding based on MAC addresses.

IPLS is similar to VPLS but assumes that customer devices are hosts or routers and that the service carries IP packets and supporting packets only. The taxonomy also distinguishes customer-edge-based VPNs, where VPN functions remain at customer devices, from provider-edge-based VPNs, where the provider edge maintains VPN state.
sections.plainLanguage: A VPWS connects two customer locations with a virtual line. VPLS joins several locations into a LAN-like service, while IPLS limits that service to IP traffic and its supporting packets.

sections.title: Customer Edge, Provider Edge, and Core
sections.content:
A customer-edge device (CE) provides the customer-side functions needed to reach a VPN service. A provider-edge device (PE) sits at the provider network’s edge and interfaces with the customer. Either role may be implemented by a device or by functions spread across devices.

A provider router (P) operates in the provider core without a direct customer interface, so it does not need VPN state. For some Layer 2 services, provider-edge work may be divided between a user-facing PE near the customer and a network-facing PE nearer the core.
sections.plainLanguage: The CE is on the customer side, the PE connects the customer to the provider, and P routers carry traffic through the provider core. These names describe roles, not necessarily separate physical boxes.

sections.title: Functions and Network Building Blocks
sections.content:
An attachment circuit connects a CE to a PE. A pseudowire carries Layer 2 traffic between PEs through a packet-switched network. Signaling lets PEs exchange information to establish pseudowires, tunnels, and the labels or other identifiers that distinguish service traffic.

For Layer 2 services, flooding sends a frame with an unknown destination to other interfaces, while MAC address learning records which interface supplied a source address. The RFC also defines terms for route distinguishers, route targets, per-VPN forwarding tables, and virtual switching instances.
sections.plainLanguage: The attachment circuit connects the customer to the provider edge. Pseudowires carry traffic between provider-edge devices, and labels help the network keep each service’s traffic distinct.
